questions.q: What does 'bounded-error' mean in the definition of BQP?
options: The algorithm must give the correct answer with probability at least 2/3 on every input, not necessarily be perfectly correct every run
The algorithm can never make a mistake, by definition
The algorithm's error grows without limit as input size increases
The algorithm only works on a bounded range of input sizes
questions.explain: Bounded-error means the per-run error probability is capped at a fixed constant below 1/2 (BQP uses 1/3), not that the algorithm is flawless. That fixed cap is exactly what makes error amplification possible.

questions.q: Why does a quantum algorithm with only a 2/3 success rate still count as reliable?
options: Running the algorithm multiple times independently and taking a majority vote drives the probability of a wrong answer down exponentially as more runs are added
A 2/3 success rate is actually already 100% reliable in practice
The success rate automatically improves over time without rerunning anything
Quantum algorithms are never run more than once by definition
questions.explain: Error amplification is the key idea: independent repeated trials with error below 1/2 combine so that the majority-vote error shrinks exponentially in the number of trials, turning a modest 2/3 guarantee into near-certainty with a modest number of extra runs.

questions.q: Which containment relationship between complexity classes is proven?
options: P ⊆ BQP ⊆ PSPACE
NP ⊆ BQP ⊆ P
PSPACE ⊆ BQP ⊆ P
BQP ⊆ P ⊆ BPP
questions.explain: P ⊆ BQP ⊆ PSPACE is proven: a quantum computer can simulate anything a classical deterministic computer does, and any BQP computation can in turn be simulated classically using only polynomial space. Whether BQP relates to NP by containment either way is still open.

questions.q: Where does integer factorization (Shor's problem) sit, stated carefully?
options: It is in BQP and in NP ∩ co-NP, and is only conjectured -- not proven -- to be outside classical P
It is proven to be outside P, and proven to be NP-complete
It is proven to require exponential time on a quantum computer as well as a classical one
It has been proven to be outside NP entirely
questions.explain: Shor's algorithm places factoring in BQP. It is also in NP ∩ co-NP because both a factorization and a primality certificate can be verified in polynomial time. Its presumed hardness for classical computers -- the basis of RSA -- is a conjecture, not a proof.

questions.q: Why is it a myth that quantum computers can solve all NP-complete problems efficiently?
options: The best known general quantum technique for brute-force search (Grover's algorithm) gives only a quadratic speedup, which still leaves the runtime exponential in input size -- no known quantum algorithm gives an exponential speedup on NP-complete problems
Quantum computers are slower than classical computers for every problem without exception
NP-complete problems have been proven to be outside BQP entirely
Quantum computers can only run algorithms that were designed before 2000
questions.explain: A quadratic speedup on an exponential search space (Grover's O(√N) vs. classical O(N)) is still exponential overall, just with a smaller exponent. Shor's exponential speedup relies on structure (hidden periodicity) that NP-complete problems like SAT are not known to have.
